newsitem.title: POLAND: FEATURE - Poland's arms makers recovering, seek exports.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Poland's arms makers recovering, seek exports.

text.p: Poland's once-mighty arms industry suffered plunging orders and financial crisis after the 1989 fall of communism but leaner, sharper firms are now hungrily hunting for export contracts.

Among the worst-hit was heavy weapons giant Bumar-Labedy in southern Poland, which used to produce hundreds of tanks a year to meet orders, set by Soviet planners, to equip Moscow's former satellites and supporters.
By 1992 the end of the Cold War had stripped Labedy of government contracts, easy credit disappeared, and the former weapons powerhouse had debts of nearly $200 million.
Poland's total arms exports shrank to less than $50 million a year from several hundred million dollars in 1988, when the country was a major armourer of the now-defunct Warsaw Pact.
After radical job cuts, modernisation and boosting non-military production, Labedy is returning to the black, reflecting a revival of the whole industry.
"Big Brother (the former Soviet Union) fell apart and...due to political and economic changes we had no domestic orders and no exports in 1991," said Labedy president Henryk Pfeifer.
"We reached the bottom but the whole sector is clearly much healthier now," he said in an interview at his firm's headquarters in the heart of heavily-polluted Silesia.
Before 1989, Poland's arms sector had more than 80 enterprises employing hundreds of thousands of people in 12 specialist branches.

It now groups 31 firms in six branches with employees counted in tens of thousands, producing armoured vehicles, helicopters, patrol boats, landing craft, rockets, small arms, ammunition, explosives and radio-location equipment.
Apart from ceasing to be a subcontractor for Soviet firms, Polish factories were hard hit by the 1991 United Nations embargo on arms sales to Iraq, a main trading partner.

But along with countrywide economic growth, which started in 1992 and reached seven percent last year, the condition of the arms industry began to improve and the chronic labour unrest which accompanied the sector's hard times is waning.
Although the arms sector's debt still totals about $550 million, an increasing number of firms have regained credit-worthiness and exports are picking up.
"In the blackest period only nine companies had credit- worthiness, now the number has increased to 25," said Jerzy Kade, defence department director at the industry ministry.

A government official familiar with the arms trade, who asked not to be named, estimated that Polish arms exports rose to about $100 million last year despite world-wide overproduction in the post-Cold War period.

"Assuming that no new products will be developed but that a system of financing arms exports is devised, I think we are capable of returning to a level of...up to $300 million a year, that is tripling our exports," the official told Reuters.
Arms sales could be boosted mainly to Poland's traditional partners -- Middle East and African countries -- and also to Far East and South American countries, the official said.
The official said Poland was also eyeing military cooperation with the countries of former Yugoslavia, once the European Union lifts its embargo on arms sales there.

Labedy, which in July lost a race with a Ukrainian firm to sell more than 300 tanks to Pakistan, hopes to sign a deal with Malaysia for about 300 of its Twardy (Hard) tanks, a development of the Soviet-designed T-72 with sophisticated armour and other improvements.
Britain's Vickers Plc, South Korea's Hyundai and a Slovak manufacturer are also competing in the Malaysian tender, expected to be completed later this year.
A new Huzar combat helicopter, being developed by the Swidnik aircraft factory, could become a hit of Polish exports. Its non-military version, named Falcon, already sells well abroad.
Huzar should be ready within 18 months, after the government picks a supplier for its anti-tank missile and avionics.
But the government official said the arms industry would never see a robust expansion without an increase in Warsaw's own defence spending and clear mid-term purchase policy.

"The defence ministry budget is set in annual cycles. Companies do know what they will be able to sell in the more distant future and cannot sign longer-term, cheaper cooperation agreements with suppliers," the official said.
A chronic lack of funds holds Poland's own purchasing back, even though politicians are keen to ensure the country pulls its weight when it joins NATO within the next few years.

Poland's military spending has shrunk by 60 percent compared with 1988, according to Jerzy Kade, head of the industry ministry's defence department. This year the defence ministry will buy military equipment worth some $280 million.
Meanwhile, the share of the arms sector's non-military output increased to nearly 80 percent from 40 percent in 1988.

Kade said the planned purchase of about 100 multi-task jet fighters, to replace some of Poland's old Soviet-made MiGs, was a big chance to technologically upgrade the arms industry by ensuring that much of the aircraft are made locally.
"Potential suppliers will be given the same rules for the deal: assembly must take place in Poland, as well as servicing and maintenance," he told Reuters.
The tender could be opened next year and completed within two years, he added. Western firms are already interested.

The U.S. firms Lockheed Martin and McDonnell Douglas are offering their F- 16s and F-18s respectively, France's Dassault Aviation proposes the Mirage 2000 and a consortium of Sweden's Saab and British Aerospace is offering the Grippen.
